\begin{proof}
If $V=\{0\}$, then $T=0$, so $T$ is a scalar multiple of the identity. Suppose $V$ contains a nonzero vector. For each nonzero $v\in V$, there is a unique scalar $a_v\in F$ such that $Tv=a_vv$.

Let $v,w\in V$ be nonzero. If $v$ and $w$ are linearly dependent, write $w=bv$ for some nonzero $b\in F$. Then
\[
a_ww=Tw=T(bv)=bTv=ba_vv=a_vw,
\]
so $a_w=a_v$. If $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent, then, for some $a_{v+w}\in F$,
\[
a_{v+w}(v+w)=T(v+w)=Tv+Tw=a_vv+a_ww.
\]
Thus
\[
(a_{v+w}-a_v)v+(a_{v+w}-a_w)w=0.
\]
Linear independence gives $a_{v+w}=a_v=a_w$. Hence all nonzero vectors have the same eigenvalue, say $a$.

Therefore $Tv=av$ for every nonzero $v$, and also $T0=0=a0$. Thus $T=aI_V$.
\end{proof}

If $V=\{0\}$, the conclusion is immediate. Otherwise choose $u\ne0$. Since every vector is an eigenvector of $T$, there is a scalar $a\in F$ with $Tu=au$.

\[
Tv=T(bu)=bTu=bau=av.
\]
If $u$ and $v$ are linearly independent, let $c\in F$ satisfy $T(u+v)=c(u+v)$. On the other hand,
\[
T(u+v)=Tu+Tv=au+Tv.
\]
Writing $Tv=dv$ for the eigenvalue $d$ associated with $v$, we obtain
\[
cu+cv=au+dv.
\]
Since $u,v$ are linearly independent, $c=a$ and $c=d$, so $d=a$ and consequently $Tv=av$.

Thus $Tv=av$ for every $v\in V$, which means $T=aI_V$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
When $V=\{0\}$, $T=0$, and the assertion holds. Assume henceforth that $V\ne\{0\}$ and choose $u\in V\setminus\{0\}$. Let $\lambda\in F$ be defined by $Tu=\lambda u$.

For any $v\in V\setminus\{0\}$, write $Tv=\mu v$ for some $\mu\in F$. If $v$ and $u$ are linearly dependent, then $v=cu$ for some $c\ne0$, and
\[
Tv=cTu=c\lambda u=\lambda v,
\]
so $\mu=\lambda$.

If $u$ and $v$ are linearly independent, then $u+v\ne0$, and for some $\nu\in F$ we have
\[
T(u+v)=\nu(u+v).
\]
By linearity,
\[
\lambda u+\mu v=Tu+Tv=T(u+v)=\nu u+\nu v.
\]
Therefore $(\lambda-\nu)u+(\mu-\nu)v=0$. Independence implies $\lambda=\nu=\mu$. Hence $Tv=\lambda v$ for every nonzero $v$; the same identity holds for $v=0$ because $T0=0$.

Thus $T=\lambda I_V$.
\end{proof}
